fable-5.1.text:
I think it's mostly true, but it depends a lot on what you mean by "idea."

So in the startup world, the saying makes sense. The idea is something like, "let's do a marketplace for this," or "let's do Uber for that." Lots of people have the same idea. And then the question is who actually builds the thing, who gets the users, who survives. In that setting, yes, the idea is cheap and the execution is everything.

But I think that in research, it's different. Or at least it has been different at various points. If you have a genuinely good idea, an idea that is actually correct, that is not cheap at all. Those are very rare. Most ideas are wrong. And the hard thing is not having ideas, it's having the right ones and being able to tell which ones are right before you've spent a year on them.

Now, I would say that the last several years in AI were a period where the saying was more true than usual. Because the recipe was known. Everyone understood that you take the transformer, you scale the data, you scale the compute, you do the pretraining. It was clear what to do. So the idea was, in some sense, cheap, and the differentiation came from execution: who can get the compute, who can build the infrastructure, who can run the training without it blowing up. That's the age of scaling, and in the age of scaling, execution really is most of it.

But I think we are moving back into something more like an age of research. Where the obvious thing has been done, and the question is what's next. And in that situation, the ideas are not cheap anymore. The bottleneck is actually the idea.

And there is one more thing I would add. I think the separation between the idea and the execution is somewhat artificial. Because very often, you don't really know what the idea is until you've tried to execute it. You have some vague notion, you try it, it doesn't work, you look at why, and then the real idea emerges from that. So the execution is also how you find out what the idea was. They're not two separate things. You need people who can do both, and those people are quite rare.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something to it, but I also think it's become less true. I saw someone put it nicely: if ideas are so cheap, how come no one's having any ideas?

It depends on what the bottleneck is. In the 90s, plenty of people had good ideas, but they didn't have the compute to show they worked. They could build a small demonstration that convinced nobody, so execution, meaning scale and resources, was what mattered. Then for a while scaling was the idea. Everyone understood the recipe: more data, more compute, bigger model, and you get something better. When everyone has the same recipe, you win on execution, because the idea is shared.

But now compute is very large, and pre-training data is finite. So we're coming back to an age of research, just with big computers. When the main question becomes "what should we do differently," the ideas start to matter a great deal again. Companies now outnumber ideas by quite a bit. Execution still matters, of course, but I think the saying undervalues how scarce genuinely new ideas are.

fable-5.text:
You know, I think this saying is a statement about a particular time, not a universal truth. If you look at the age of scaling — let's say from GPT-3 up through the recent past — the saying was mostly correct, because everyone knew what the idea was. The idea was: scale the transformer, get more compute, get more data. When the idea is known and shared by everyone, then of course the difference between companies is execution. Who can build the bigger cluster, who can get the data pipeline working, who can make the training run not diverge. Execution was everything because the idea was free.

But the saying has an interesting problem, which is: if ideas are so cheap, how come there are so few of them? Deep learning itself was an idea. That the neural network should be big, that you should train it end to end on a lot of data — in 2010 almost nobody believed this. That idea, held with conviction, was worth a great deal, and execution without it would have gotten you nowhere.

And I think we are now moving back into a time where this matters. Compute is very large now. Everyone has a lot of compute, relatively speaking. Data is becoming the constraint. So the differentiator is shifting back from execution to ideas — we are going from the age of scaling back to the age of research. And in research, the scarce thing is not effort, it's having the right belief before it's obvious, and the taste to know which of your hundred ideas is the one worth betting on. So I'd say: ideas are cheap when you're doing what everyone else is doing. When you're not, they're the whole thing.

opus-5.text:
I think that saying is more a statement about business than about research. If you are building a company where everyone already agrees on what the product should be, then yes, the bottleneck is execution, because the idea is not actually doing any work for you. But in research it's very different. In research, the thing you're looking for is precisely the idea, and most ideas are wrong, and the hard part is having the taste to know which direction is even worth the effort of executing on.

I'd say you need both, but they're not symmetric. Execution without the right idea gets you a very well-engineered thing that doesn't matter. And there have been cases where the whole thing turned on a very small number of ideas. Deep learning plus big data plus compute — that's an idea, and it was not obvious, and a lot of very capable people spent years executing beautifully on other paradigms that were not going to work. The ResNet is an idea. The transformer is an idea. You can't execute your way to those.

The reason people say ideas are cheap, I think, is that they've been exposed to a lot of bad ideas, which really are cheap and abundant. Someone tells you "we should do X," and it's underspecified, and it hasn't been pressure-tested, and the person saying it has no sense of whether it's true. That's not what I mean by an idea. A good idea comes with a reason to believe it, some intuition about why the world should work this way. Those are rare. And so my experience has been close to the opposite: the ideas are the scarce thing, and there are a lot of people who can execute, and the real question is what you point them at.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's true in some sense, but it's also incomplete. People say it as if ideas were abundant and the only scarce thing were the grind of building them. But if ideas were really that cheap, you'd expect everyone to be overflowing with good ones. They aren't. Good ideas, the kind that change what people do, are rare. There's a line I like, something like: if ideas are so cheap, why does no one have any?

Part of the problem is that an idea doesn't arrive labeled as good. Most ideas sound plausible, and most of them don't work. So a lot of what we call execution is really how you find out whether an idea is any good. You build it, run the experiment, and see what the world says. In that sense the two are tangled together. The experiment is part of how the idea becomes an idea you can trust.

There's also a different kind of idea. It isn't a clever trick but a conviction about how things should work, and it often looks wrong or even silly at first. To pursue it you need something close to what I'd call top-down belief. You believe the thing should work because of a certain aesthetic, a sense of beauty, simplicity, and correctness, and that belief keeps you going when the data says no. Most of the time the data is telling you you're wrong. Sometimes it's just that you have a bug. Telling those two situations apart is hard, and it's part of why good research is hard.

So I'd put it this way. Execution matters a great deal, and a mediocre idea well executed will often beat a great idea executed badly. But I wouldn't call ideas cheap. The right ideas are very valuable, and finding them is the part that's rare.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the saying is half right, and the half that's wrong matters. Ideas are cheap in the sense that lots of people have the same thought at the same time. Most of the time, the thing you're excited about has already occurred to someone else. But a good idea that's actually right is rare, and you usually can't tell it's right until you've spent a long time working on it. So the value isn't really in the idea as a sentence. It's in the conviction to keep working on something that looks wrong or half-formed to everyone else.

Execution matters, but I'd describe it differently. It's less about grinding through a plan and more about the loop between trying something and learning from what happens. A lot of progress comes from running the experiment, looking closely at the result, and realizing the question you asked was slightly off. If you can't iterate that quickly and honestly, even a great idea stays theoretical.

So I'd say ideas aren't cheap, they're just easy to have. The hard part is choosing the few that deserve a lot of effort and then being willing to be surprised by what the effort shows you.

astra-6.text:
I think that saying is overstated. It’s true that you can have an idea that sounds good, and then all the difficulty is in making it work. But choosing what to work on is itself extremely important. You can execute very well on something that turns out not to matter.

And I don’t think ideas and execution are so separate. When you’re executing, you’re constantly encountering problems, and you need ideas to solve those problems. It’s not one idea at the beginning followed by purely mechanical work.

So I would say: some ideas are cheap. A really good idea, one that points you in a productive direction that wasn’t obvious before, can be very valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it undersells ideas. Execution is very important, of course. But the idea determines where you put your effort. You can spend an enormous amount of effort pursuing something that simply won’t work. An insight that tells you where to look can save you years.

There is also a question of what we mean by an idea. If the idea is, “Let’s build an AI company,” then, yes, many people can have that idea. But if it’s a specific insight into why something should work, something that other people haven’t understood, that can be extremely valuable.

And execution itself involves having ideas. You encounter a problem, you need to understand it, you need to find a way around it. So I find the separation a little artificial. You need good judgment about what to do, and then you need the persistence and ability to actually do it.

luna-5.6.text:
I think it’s directionally true, but it’s too simplistic. Execution is absolutely essential—an idea that never becomes a system, a product, or an experiment has no practical value. But the right ideas are not cheap. In a new field, identifying the crucial idea can be the hardest part, because it determines what you build, what you measure, and where you spend years of effort.

Also, execution and ideas are not really separate. Good execution often reveals better ideas, and a good idea can make execution dramatically easier. So I would say: mediocre ideas are cheap, and execution matters enormously—but exceptional ideas, especially the ones that change what is possible, are extraordinarily valuable.
